newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--Wheat soars as Europe cuts exports, pork and coffee gain.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Wheat soars as Europe cuts exports, pork and coffee gain.

text.p: Wheat prices soared on Thursday as export prospects improved after the European Union said it would suspend its weekly sales tenders.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery soared the allowable 20-cent per bushel daily limit on the news and closed at $4.25-1/4, up 18-1/2 cents and the highest closing price since September 3.

Dry weather in European wheat areas, especially in France, was cited as a key factor halting weekly export tenders by the European Commission, where the bulk of Europe's 9.6 million metric tons of wheat exports since last July have been sold.
"The EU action is really the catalyst for this," said Charlie Sernatinger, analyst at E.D. and F. Man International.
"It exacerbates an already tight supply situation worldwide. Basically, it is just us and Canada as the sole remaining sellers in the world until October."

Wheat prices are also being supported by a freeze last weekend in the High Plains that agronomists said severely damaged the winter wheat just now coming out of dormancy. The wheat will be harvested starting in June.
Flooding in the Dakotas also prompted worries that spring wheat planting will be delayed or abandoned in many areas.

Joe Victor, vice president of marketing for Allendale Inc, said Thursday's EU action was preceded on Monday by the EU's trimming its tariff duty on some wheat imports, a clear sign it was concerned about dry weather cutting the current crop.
"They have to make sure they have enough domestic supplies to feed their own countries," Victor said.
Weekly wheat export sales reported on Thursday by the U.S. Agriculture Department were a strong 263,900 tons, against trade estimates of 100,000 to 200,000 tons.

Soybeans for May delivery closed 6-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $8.38-1/2 and May soybean meal also closed strong at $276.20 a ton, up $2.90. Both were supported by stronger than expected weekly exports.
Booming pork exports, especially to Japan, also pushed prices higher at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
Pork bellies for May delivery closed up the allowable 3.00 cent a pound daily limit at 87.55 cents and the June lean hog contract soared the daily 2.00 cent a pound limit to close at 85.45 cents.

Brisk demand for pork bellies, the raw material for bacon, reflected confirmation by Japanese trading houses that they were buying U.S. bellies following a sudden halt to Taiwanese pork exports last month due to a disease outbreak.
Japanese traders told Reuters they would buy U.S. bellies until late May to fill needs into the end of the year.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures closed higher on carryover interest from Tuesday's surprising report of smaller than expected warehouse coffee stocks in the United States.
Coffee for May delivery closed at 209.80 cents, up 1.75 cents.

Prices jumped after a monthly report from the Green Coffee Association of New York said stocks of coffee in U.S. warehouses rose in March by only 111,000 132-pound bags to 1,657,000 bags, a much smaller buildup than expected.

"Sentiment is still bullish after the Green Coffee Association stocks data impacted Wednesday, but there was no follow-through buying today and volumes were lower," Refco New York analyst Anne Prendergast said.

"The GCA stocks are only voluntarily reported warehouse stocks and don't include roaster stocks, so we suspect inventories may be higher given the surge in Latin American exports in recent months," she said.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices eked out minor gains on expectations that rising gasoline demand would help prices this spring. Gasoline for May delivery ended up 0.32 cent at 60.70 cents a gallon.

"I think the price action reflects the fact that gasoline inventories are still below a year ago and the demand is picking up," said John Bradberry, vice president of Transmontaigne Products Services Inc, a petroleum distributor in Fayetteville, Arkansas.
Crude oil for May delivery ended 7 cents a barrel higher at $19.42 and May heating oil closed up 0.52 cent at 54.00 cents a gallon.
Unseasonably cold weather in much of the United States has stalled the usual seasonal rise in gasoline demand leading up to the summer vacation season.
